items.caption:
This might be one of the coolest AI models I’ve seen all year.

Tencent’s new WorldClaw model can generate an entire editable 3D world from a prompt — not just the environment, but every individual object inside it.

Trees, buildings, carts, lamp posts, terrain, they’re all generated as separate 3D assets you can actually work with.

Under the hood, it combines image generation, segmentation, and Tencent’s Hunyuan 2D-to-3D tech to turn a generated scene into a full collection of 3D objects.

And the use cases could get really interesting.

You could imagine generating game environments in minutes, building virtual worlds for simulations, or even creating environments where robots can train before they ever enter the real world.

Unfortunately we can’t actually play with this model yet, but this is absolutely one I’m keeping an eye on.

items.caption:
Comment “AI” and I’ll send you the link to try them all.

Here’s everything that happened in AI this week in 60 seconds:

At number 6, OpenViking solves the memory problem for AI agents. It’s an open-source context database that gives an agent one place to keep knowledge, user memories and reusable experience. 

Number 5, Google open-sourced ARTEMIS, which turns prompts into real phone automations. It plugs straight into Codex, Claude Code and Antigravity over MCP, and it captures the logs and screenshots while it works.

Number 4, PrismML released Ternary Bonsai 2, a 27-billion-parameter reasoning model with a 262,000-token context. Ternary compression shrinks it enough to run on your own machine, with coding, math, tool calling and image understanding.

Number 3, AWS open-sourced Pizza Bot, an inbox for background AI agents. Your agents keep running while you do something else, and everything they finish or need you to approve shows up like email. It works on Mac, Windows and Linux.

Number 2, Zai dropped GLM-5.3 FlashX. Comes with 320 billion parameters, natively multimodal, a million-token context, 200 tokens a second, and it’s free and private on your own hardware.

And at number 1, Unsloth Studio now lets you fine-tune 500-plus open models in a free Google Colab. No code, just pick a model, upload your data and hit train, then export it and run it locally.

items.creator: dailyhistoryclips
items.caption:
Glenn Gould was one of the great pianists of the twentieth century, and he sang while he played. Not quietly. A wordless humming that followed whatever line his hands were on, and it is there on almost every record he made.

Columbia’s engineers spent years trying to get rid of it. They pulled the microphones further from his face, changed the angles, tried putting a screen between him and the keyboard. Nothing worked. There was nowhere to put a microphone that could hear the piano but not the man bent over it.

Gould never treated it as a fault. He said he was not so much playing the music as thinking it, and the voice was part of the thinking.

He traced the habit back to his childhood, to an afternoon when the family vacuum cleaner was running while he practised. The noise swallowed the piano completely, and he realised he could hear the piece more clearly in his head than through his ears. He learned everything that way afterwards, away from the instrument, so by the time he sat down the music was already sounding inside him. The humming was just the overflow.

Put on his Goldberg Variations and there is a second instrument in the room, slightly out of tune with the first.

👉 Join the community @dailyhistoryclips

items.creator: ryanlpeterman
items.caption:
The only unbreakable law in software engineering

Casey Muratori (Video Game Dev & Creator): What is the only unbreakable law in software engineering? The only thing I've seen that feels like a real law to me is the thing I cover in this lecture, which is Conway's law.

And it is that if you would like to organize a series, like a set of people to work on something, or in the modern parlance, let's say agents, if you need to partition a problem into a set of workers in this way where the communication between those workers is slower than their own internal computation ability, when you start to tackle a problem, in order to get the benefits of that parallelization, you will have to make decisions about who is working on what.

Once you've made that decision, you have now locked in the fact that that the iteration on the design will be slower across that boundary than it is interior to either of the two parts. One way the rule is pithily stated is products look like the org chart, right?

But that's not exactly what it says. But that's a downstream consequence and boy do you ever see it in the real world.

For the full conversation, you can search Casey Muratori on my YouTube, Spotify or Apple Podcasts (link in bio)

Banks can issue stablecoins now, and they keep the interest on your cash.

Find out how we’re taking advantage of this inside the group. Link in bio, a dollar a month.

The GENIUS Act, the US stablecoin law, lets banks create their own stablecoins.

You give the bank $100,000 and get $100,000 in stablecoins back. The bank holds your cash in things like short term Treasury bills, which are loans to the US government, and it keeps the interest. The law doesn’t let it pay that interest to you.

The bank can also lend those Treasury bills out in short loans called repurchase agreements, so it can raise cash fast when people cash out.

Your stablecoin can go to work too. You can trade it for tokenized Treasuries, which are Treasury bills on the blockchain. One of those funds, USYC, is even accepted as collateral for big trading clients on Binance, a major crypto exchange.

Right now a 3 month Treasury bill pays about 4%. A lot of stablecoin money ends up flowing into US government debt.

Follow so you catch the next move early.

items.creator: alexanderelorenzo
items.caption:
They are fighting over your data and you are not in the room.

We break down where AI and crypto actually connect inside the group. Link in bio or skool.com/coinpicksgenesis. A dollar a month.

Right now the biggest AI companies on earth are in court over scraping. Anthropic settled with authors for around 1.5 billion dollars last September. The New York Times case against OpenAI has been sitting open since December 2023.

Everybody frames it as a copyright fight. It isn’t. Strip it all the way down and the websites just want to get paid for what’s being taken from them.

Now the part almost nobody knows. There’s a payment slot that was written into the internet back around 1991 and then sat there unused for over thirty years. In 2025 they switched it on. It’s called x402.

What that means is you can drop it into a website and any AI agent that wants to scrape your data has to pay a toll to get through. A toll booth on your own information, which flat out did not exist before.

So the lawsuits are the loud version of this fight. The quiet version is an entire payment layer getting built underneath the internet while everybody argues in court.

And your data is the thing they’re arguing about.

There’s a twelve hundred dollar grant with no proposal, no plan, and no artist statement. You email them pictures. That’s the whole application.

It’s called Artist Grant. Running since 2017, they give $1,200 unrestricted to one visual artist three times a year. Unrestricted meaning nobody tells you what to spend it on.

The actual application: you send an email. In it, either a link to your website, or 3 to 5 images of your work plus a short bio. You tell them whether they can share your work on their social media. That’s it. Their own site says, and I’m quoting, no grant proposal required.

Open to visual artists anywhere in the world, 18 and over. Painting, drawing, sculpture, ceramics, printmaking, photography, mixed media, installation.

The honest bits, because I’d rather you knew: there’s a $30 application fee, it isn’t for film, music, theatre or dance, and past winners can’t win again.

Three deadlines a year, so there’s always one coming. Miss the next and there’s another behind it.

Here’s what I want you to take from this. You’ve spent years telling yourself you can’t apply for funding because you haven’t got the CV, or the statement, or the right words. This one wants none of that. It wants to see the work. Which is the only thing you already have.

You can start selling prints of a painting you already own tonight. No printer, no stock, no money up front.

Here’s the bit nobody explains. There are companies that print and post the thing for you. You upload a photo, you set your price, and when someone orders, they print it, pack it, ship it and send you the difference. You never touch a box. Printful, Gelato and Fine Art America all work roughly like this and none charge you to open an account.

So the only real job is the photograph:

Flat, in daylight, near a window. Overcast is better than sun.
No flash.
Phone straight on, propped on books if you’ve no tripod. Not at an angle.
Crop to the edge of the canvas.

A good phone photo in good light beats a bad photo from an expensive camera every time.

And don’t list one painting, list ten. A print shop with one product looks like a mistake. A print shop with ten looks like a shop.

That painting you sold three years ago and still think about? Unless you signed something saying otherwise, you still own the right to print it.

Send this to an artist who’s been meaning to do this for two years.

items.creator: foundedceo
items.caption:
Claude Code creator Boris Cherny says the model can actually become slightly more intelligent when its system prompts are removed. Anthropic discovered this through ablation testing, where the team strips away instructions and tool prompts to measure what is genuinely improving the model. The surprising result was that more prompting didn’t always produce more intelligence. In some cases, the additional instructions were constraining what the model could do.

For founders and developers building with AI, this is a useful reminder that prompting is part of the product architecture. Every instruction added to an agent can shape its behavior, narrow its decision-making, and influence how well it handles problems outside the exact workflow you designed. The goal is to give the model enough context to behave reliably without burying its underlying capabilities under unnecessary instructions.

They will simply trust it more.

They will stay longer.

They will pay closer attention.

And they will remember it after they leave.

That is the real power of high-level design.

items.creator: jg.engineers
items.caption:
🔧 4 GitHub repos to explore instead of scrolling ↓↓

Save this post for later!

⚙️ FREECAD — github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD
What it is: A fully open source parametric 3D CAD tool built for mechanical engineering
What you’ll find: The actual source code behind a professional grade CAD application — geometry kernels, constraint solvers, FEA integration, the lot
Why pull it apart: Reading how a real CAD tool is built teaches you more about design intent and parametric modelling than any tutorial ever will. Free to download and use right now.

🌊 OPENFOAM — github.com/OpenFOAM
What it is: The industry standard open source CFD simulation engine used by aerospace, automotive and energy companies worldwide
What you’ll find: Fluid dynamics solvers, mesh tools and simulation cases you can run on your own machine
Why pull it apart: Every time you design something that moves through air or fluid this is what the professionals use to validate it. Pull a tutorial case apart and run it. You will understand flow, pressure and heat transfer in a completely different way.

🤖 LEROBOT — github.com/huggingface/lerobot
What it is: Hugging Face’s open source robotics framework — hardware files, firmware, AI training tools all in one repo
What you’ll find: Full design files for the SO-101 robot arm, reinforcement learning and imitation learning code, datasets and pre-trained models
Why pull it apart: This is the most accessible on-ramp into AI controlled physical hardware available right now. Print the arm, run the code, train it to pick something up. The entire stack is open source.

🚁 JPL OPEN SOURCE ROVER — github.com/nasa-jpl/open-source-rover
What it is: NASA’s open source scaled down version of the Mars rover — designed entirely from consumer off the shelf parts
What you’ll find: Full mechanical design files, electronics schematics, firmware and build documentation
Why pull it apart: NASA built this specifically for people who want to learn mechanical engineering, electronics and software through a real build. If it is good enough for JPL it is good enough to learn from.

Follow for more ↓

#engineer #github

items.creator: politicallyhomeless1982
items.caption:
There Is No Democracy Without Journalism

Scott Pelley was asked about President Trump reportedly calling him a “stiff” and suggesting he was among people who “don’t care about the country.”

His response wasn’t about politics.

It was about service.

Pelley pointed to years spent covering wars alongside American troops in Iraq, Afghanistan, and Kuwait before making a broader point:

“There is no democracy without journalism. It can’t be done.”

Whether you agree with a journalist’s reporting or not, a free press is one of the institutions that allows citizens to hold power accountable.

The danger comes when we begin treating information like a menu—accepting facts from people we like and dismissing them from people we don’t.

We don’t build an informed society by hearing only voices that confirm what we already believe.

The test of a free press isn’t whether journalists tell us what we want to hear. It’s whether they are free to report facts that challenge us, our political tribe, or those in power.

A democracy requires voters.

A democracy requires elections.

A democracy requires an informed public.

And an informed public requires journalism.

Source: Scott Pelley interview with Lulu Garcia-Navarro, The New York Times.

#ScottPelley #Journalism #FirstAmendment #FreePress #Democracy

items.creator: creativeflairhq
items.caption:
There are five numbers that decide what your work is actually worth. Most artists guess all five, then blame the market.

It is not your talent. It is your maths.

One. Your size number. Height plus width in inches, times one rate you set and use on everything.

Two. Your cost floor. Materials, framing, and the commission a gallery takes, often half. Clear it or you are paying to give the work away.

Three. Your comparable. Three artists with a CV like yours. Not the ones you admire. The ones level with you. That band is your real market.

Four. Your consistency number. The same formula on every piece, so a collector can predict your prices. Random numbers read as an artist who does not know their own worth.

Five. Your floor you will not break. Decided before anyone asks, because in the room you will cave. A discount comes off the value. It never gets added to the sale.

Pricing is not a feeling you have on the day. It is five numbers you work out once and hold.

Guess them and you look like a hobby. Set them and you look like a career.

Send this to the artist still pricing by vibes.

#ArtPricing #CreativeFlair #ArtistAdvice #SellingArt #EmergingArtist

Tracing a path from his pioneering interactive media works to new projects inspired by the sacred geometry of Tibetan thangka painting, Snibbe reflects on how art, technology, and contemplative practice can reveal deeper qualities of mind and experience. The talk will conclude with a brief guided meditation paired with a new work of art.

Snibbe’s career has included exhibitions at MoMA, the Whitney Museum of American Art, London’s Institute of Contemporary Art, SFMOMA, and Tokyo’s Intercommunications Center. His recent book, How to Train a Happy Mind, with a foreword by the Dalai Lama, shares the little-known techniques of analytical meditation in a nonreligious form.

This event is presented in conjunction with the if then, amen group exhibition at tiat. if then, amen is a group exhibition exploring computational divinity and networked belief systems in the age of intelligent machines, on display through May 11th in tiat’s gallery at 151 Powell St. 📍

tiat is the intersection of art and technology! tiat is a gallery for artworks using technology as a medium and gathering place for creative technologists to experiment, exhibit, and expand their practice. ⋆౨ৎ˚⟡˖

items.creator: deeplearnai
items.caption:
Spam calls are one of the most annoying problems on the internet era. But surprisingly, a U.S. law from 1991 might allow you to earn up to $1,500 for each illegal robocall.

The problem is that most robocallers hide behind fake names, spoofed phone numbers, and anonymous operations, making it almost impossible for consumers to identify them.

That’s where technology - and increasingly AI - comes in.

Tools like DoNotPay created a virtual credit card system designed to uncover the real identity of spam callers. When a robocaller tries to sell you something, you give them the virtual card. When they attempt to process the payment, the payment network reveals the business name, address, and phone number behind the call.

That information can then be used to automatically generate legal claims under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act.

One user reportedly turned this into a full-time strategy, earning nearly $100,000 from robocall lawsuits.

AI isn’t just automating tasks - it’s helping people fight back.

Follow @deeplearnai for daily insights on AI, automation, and the future of technology.

Credits: 

Video : Relentless Podcast ti_morse

Speaker :  Joshua Browder, founder & CEO of DoNotPay

items.creator: aiproductlabs
items.caption:
LingBot-Map — Autoregressive 3D world understanding in real time

Open-source GitHub project by Ant Group’s Robbyant team. A feed-forward 3D foundation model designed for streaming reconstruction from video.

What makes it different:
• Processes scenes sequentially (no full video required upfront)
• Reconstructs camera pose and dense 3D geometry in real time from a single RGB stream
• Uses a Geometric Context Transformer combining spatial grounding, geometry understanding, and temporal memory

Core capabilities:
• Real-time streaming inference (~20 FPS) across long sequences
• Continuous mapping and localization (SLAM-like behavior)
• Works directly from live video or image streams
• Handles long-range consistency and drift correction
• Efficient transformer architecture with KV-cache for scalability

Why it matters:
Turns raw video into live 3D understanding, enabling real-time spatial intelligence for robotics, autonomous systems, and AR/VR.

items.creator: ojrgb
items.caption:
“Claude can do this in 10 minutes!” Is a caption I see a LOT rn and I definitely have mixed feelings about it. On one hand it’s awesome seeing so many people experience the magic of software engineering. On the other hand I am (a little?) concerned about the watering down of what is essentially a very complicated magic trick to a “caricature” of what it really is. I get my kicks out of feeling like I pushed the envelope and (maybe?) that gives me the appreciation for the folks who laid the foundation and did the research that enabled me to do what I do. I’m just hoping that anyone who picks it up now develops a real love for it and doesn’t just use it for transient clout… and this isn’t to say that it’s wrong to generate something that gives you joy with AI! it does mean that if you did it in 10 minutes then everyone could, and I’m selfishly hoping you’ll use that as a springboard to push this space into new realms. Rant over! LOL. Anyways, lmk what you think in the comments. Maybe I’m fully in “old man yells at clouds” territory 🤣

Also, happy 100 posts to me! Woohoo!!!

I’ve been dying to get Claude Voice mode on mobile connected to Claude Code, and I finally figured out a (hacky) way to do it. 

Which means you can access Claude Code in a way that is: Conversational, Hands-Free, and Mobile!

It allows me to walk around with my AirPods in and brainstorm with Claude Voice Mode whenever I have an idea, without taking my phone out of my pocket. Then I just tell Voice Claude to send a task to Claude Code and it starts working on it. I do my best thinking when I’m walking outside, so this has been a desire of mine since chatGPT voice mode came out.

This is obviously something that is best left to the big AI companies to do properly, since they own both ends of this process, and I think it’s crazy they haven’t already. But until then, I’ll be using this hack when I want to get away from my desk but still noodle on a project.

items.caption:
You may or may not like this, but research is one of the most powerful tools in your toolkit. 

Coming up with good ideas and being creative is driven by intuition and fuelled by research, insight and knowledge. 

Two do my favourite books on research and the creative process are:

A Technique for Producing Ideas, by James Webb Young. Talks about a five step process for generating really powerful ideas, and various other creative techniques. 

Hit Makers: The Science of Popularity, by Derek Thompson, reflects on the turning points for content distribution, psychology of popularity (going viral) and really interesting network effect of dark broadcasts.
